questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Define scarcity in an engineering design brief
questions.stem: An engineer has 40 hours and must choose between two product features this sprint.

options.text: The situation is one of scarcity because wants exceed the available 40 hours
options.misconception: confuses scarcity with a simple lack of money

options.text: The situation is not scarcity because only two features are involved
options.misconception: thinks scarcity requires many competing wants

options.text: Scarcity means limited resources force a choice among competing uses
Scarcity applies only when materials run out completely
options.misconception: limits scarcity to total depletion of inputs

questions.explanation: Scarcity is the condition that resources are limited relative to wants, forcing choices. It holds even with just two features and forty hours. The other options misstate the scope or trigger of scarcity.
questions.hint: Scarcity is about limited resources, not zero resources.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Identify the opportunity cost of a design choice
questions.stem: A team spends 5000 dollars on a prototype instead of a marketing campaign that would have earned 7200 dollars.
questions.explanation: The opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative forgone, which is the 7200 dollars from marketing. The spent amount is a sunk cost, not the opportunity cost.
questions.hint: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative forgone.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Describe what points inside the production possibilities frontier represent for a factory.

answer.exemplar: Points inside the frontier represent inefficient production, where the factory uses its resources without reaching full potential and could produce more of at least one good without sacrificing the other.

questions.explanation: Interior points signal inefficiency or underutilized resources. Points on the curve are efficient, and points outside are unattainable with current resources and technology.
questions.hint: Interior means resources are not fully or efficiently used.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.learningObjective: Recognize a cause of economic growth
questions.stem: Which change would shift an economy's production possibilities frontier outward?

options.text: A hurricane destroys half the factory capital
options.misconception: confuses a negative shock with growth

options.text: A new manufacturing process raises labor productivity
A rise in the price of exported goods
options.misconception: confuses price changes with productive capacity

options.text: A temporary shortage of skilled workers
options.misconception: mistakes a short-run constraint for capacity change

questions.explanation: Economic growth comes from more or better resources or technology, shifting the frontier outward. A productivity-raising process does this. Price changes and shortages do not expand capacity.
questions.hint: Growth needs more or better resources or technology.

questions.stem: A plant produces goods at lowest unit cost but makes items no buyer wants.

It is allocatively efficient but not productively efficient
It is both productively and allocatively efficient
options.misconception: assumes low cost implies social value

options.text: It is neither efficient in any sense
options.misconception: ignores that cost minimization still holds

questions.explanation: Lowest unit cost means productive efficiency. Making unwanted goods means allocative efficiency fails because resources do not match preferences. The plant hits one but not the other.
questions.hint: Productive is about cost; allocative is about wants.

questions.stem: A designer has 240 dollars and each unit of steel costs 12 dollars. What is the maximum steel units purchasable?

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Why does choosing one engineering design always involve giving something up?

answer.exemplar: Because resources such as time, money, and materials are scarce, any choice to use them for one design removes them from another possible use, creating a tradeoff.

questions.explanation: Scarcity means resources have competing uses. Choosing one use necessarily denies the alternative, so tradeoffs are unavoidable. This is the core logic of opportunity cost.
questions.hint: Scarcity forces every choice to deny an alternative.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A firm redirects current output into new machinery rather than consumption goods.

options.text: This reduces both current and future output
options.misconception: ignores that capital raises future capacity

options.text: This sacrifices current consumption to raise future production
This has no effect on long-run output
options.misconception: assumes capital is irrelevant to capacity

options.text: This only changes prices, not quantities

questions.explanation: Investment in machinery is a current sacrifice of consumption goods that expands future productive capacity. It shifts the frontier outward over time. The other options deny this link.
questions.hint: Investment trades present consumption for future capacity.

There is no scarcity if the client pays more

questions.explanation: Time is scarce relative to the two competing wants, so a choice is forced. Scarcity does not require money or multiple people. Paying more cannot create more hours.
questions.hint: Time itself is a scarce resource.

stimulus.body: A team can build 12 units of feature X or 8 units of feature Y with the same labor. Current plan builds 6 units of X.

questions.stem: What is the opportunity cost of the 6 units of X already built?

options.text: 6 units of Y, since half the labor went to X
options.misconception: assumes linear proportion without checking rate

options.text: 4 units of Y, based on the 12-to-8 tradeoff rate
8 units of Y, the full alternative output
options.misconception: uses the total alternative rather than the forgone portion

options.text: 12 units of X, confusing output with cost
options.misconception: mistakes the chosen output for the cost

questions.explanation: The tradeoff rate is 12 X for 8 Y, so one X costs two-thirds of a Y. Six X cost four Y. The forgone Y is four units, not the full eight.
questions.hint: Use the tradeoff rate to convert X into Y.

options.text: Producing 90 chairs and 40 tables is efficient
options.misconception: labels an interior point as efficient

options.text: Producing 120 chairs and 60 tables is unattainable now
Producing 80 chairs and 40 tables is unattainable now

questions.explanation: Points outside the frontier need more resources or better technology. One hundred twenty chairs and sixty tables exceeds current capacity. Interior points are attainable but inefficient.
questions.hint: Outside the frontier means beyond current capacity.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: What does it mean for a factory to be productively efficient?

answer.exemplar: It means the factory produces the maximum output from given resources, or the minimum cost for a given output, so no waste remains in the production process.

questions.explanation: Productive efficiency is about cost minimization for a given output, not about matching preferences. It is achieved when no resource is wasted and all inputs are fully employed.
questions.hint: Productive efficiency is minimum cost for given output.

The quantity of each good consumed
The consumer's income after taxes

questions.stem: How does investing in new tools affect an economy's production possibilities?

answer.exemplar: Investing in new tools raises future productivity and expands the production possibilities frontier outward, though it may reduce current consumption.

questions.explanation: Investment adds capital and technology, increasing future capacity. The tradeoff is lower present consumption for higher future output. This is the engine of growth.
questions.hint: Investment expands future capacity at a present cost.

Scarcity is absent because the firm has cash
Scarcity only applies to labor, not capital

options.text: Scarcity ends once revenue arrives
options.misconception: confuses future income with present limits

questions.explanation: Even with cash, wants exceed the budget, so scarcity holds. Money does not remove scarcity; it is itself a scarce resource. Future revenue does not change present limits.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Why is the production possibilities frontier usually bowed outward?

answer.exemplar: Because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods, so shifting resources raises the opportunity cost, producing increasing marginal cost and a bowed-out shape.

questions.explanation: Unequal resource suitability means opportunity cost rises as more of one good is produced. This increasing cost bows the frontier outward rather than a straight line.
questions.hint: Rising opportunity cost bows the frontier outward.

questions.explanation: Time is scarce, so spending it on speed leaves less for quality assurance. The tradeoff persists unless resources expand. This mirrors the production possibilities logic.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: How does a new production technology affect economic growth?

answer.exemplar: It raises output per unit of input, shifting the production possibilities frontier outward and enabling more goods without more resources.

questions.explanation: Technology improves productivity, expanding capacity. More output becomes possible from the same inputs, which is the definition of growth via technology.
questions.hint: Technology raises productivity and expands capacity.

questions.hint: Divide output by input.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: What is a budget constraint in consumer choice?

answer.exemplar: A budget constraint is the set of all combinations of goods a consumer can afford given prices and income, forming a line whose slope reflects relative prices.

questions.explanation: It limits affordable bundles to those within income. The line's intercepts show maximum single-good quantities and its slope shows the tradeoff rate.
questions.hint: It limits affordable bundles given prices and income.

questions.explanation: Thirty sensors and fifteen actuators is half of each maximum, an interior point. The lab could raise one good without sacrificing the other, so it is inefficient.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: How does scarcity differ from a shortage?

answer.exemplar: Scarcity is permanent and universal because resources are limited relative to wants, while a shortage is temporary and occurs when price is below equilibrium.

questions.explanation: Scarcity is a timeless condition of limited resources. A shortage is a market outcome at a specific price and can be resolved by price adjustment.
questions.hint: Scarcity is permanent; shortages are temporary price outcomes.

questions.explanation: Allocative efficiency matches output to preferences. It occurs when marginal benefit equals marginal cost, not merely when cost is minimized.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Moving along the frontier, 15 more units of X cost 6 units of Y. What is the per-unit cost of X in Y?
questions.explanation: Per-unit cost equals 6 Y divided by 15 X, or 0.4 Y per X. The ratio gives the marginal opportunity cost.
questions.hint: Divide forgone Y by gained X.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: How does better education contribute to economic growth?

answer.exemplar: Better education raises worker productivity and human capital, expanding output per worker and shifting the production possibilities frontier outward.

questions.explanation: Education improves human capital, raising productivity. Higher productivity expands capacity, which is economic growth.
questions.hint: Education raises human capital and productivity.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A process costs 200 dollars to produce 50 units. What is cost per unit?
questions.explanation: Cost per unit equals 200 dollars divided by 50 units, or 4 dollars per unit. Lower cost per unit means higher productive efficiency.
questions.hint: Divide total cost by units produced.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: If income rises while prices stay fixed, the budget line does what?

options.text: Shifts outward in parallel
Rotates around the origin
options.misconception: confuses income change with price change

options.text: Shifts inward in parallel
Becomes steeper
options.misconception: confuses income change with relative price change

questions.explanation: Higher income shifts the budget line outward in parallel because both intercepts rise while the slope, the price ratio, stays fixed.
questions.hint: Income changes shift; price changes rotate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A designer must choose between a lighter material and a cheaper one for a part.

options.text: There is no tradeoff because both are valid
The tradeoff is weight versus cost
The tradeoff is only about aesthetics
The tradeoff disappears with a bigger budget

questions.explanation: The competing attributes are weight and cost, so the tradeoff is between them. A bigger budget relaxes but does not eliminate the tradeoff if constraints remain.
questions.hint: Name the two competing attributes.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Why must investment exceed depreciation for capital to grow?

answer.exemplar: Net capital growth occurs only when new investment replaces worn-out capital and adds more, so investment must exceed depreciation.

questions.explanation: Depreciation erodes the capital stock. Investment must first replace it and then add net new capital for growth to occur.
questions.hint: Investment must replace worn capital and add more.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: A worker has 8 hours and two tasks needing 5 and 6 hours. How many hours short is the worker?
questions.explanation: The tasks need 11 hours combined but only 8 are available, so the worker is 3 hours short. Scarcity of time forces a choice.
questions.hint: Subtract available hours from total needed.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS

stimulus.body: A team can produce 18 units of A or 12 units of B per day. They choose to produce 9 units of A.

questions.stem: What is the opportunity cost of the 9 units of A?

options.text: 6 units of B
12 units of B
9 units of B
18 units of A

questions.explanation: The rate is 18 A for 12 B, so one A costs two-thirds B. Nine A cost 6 B. The forgone output is six units.
questions.hint: Convert chosen A into forgone B using the rate.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: What causes an inward shift of the production possibilities frontier?

answer.exemplar: A loss of resources or technology, such as natural disaster or capital destruction, reduces capacity and shifts the frontier inward.

questions.explanation: Inward shifts reflect reduced capacity from resource loss or technological decline. Growth is the opposite, an outward shift.
questions.hint: Resource or technology loss shifts it inward.

questions.subject: MACROECONOMICS
questions.stem: Name the main sources of economic growth for an economy.

answer.exemplar: More labor, more capital, better technology, and improved human capital raise output per worker and expand the production possibilities frontier.

questions.explanation: Growth comes from expanding resources and improving technology and human capital. These raise productivity and shift the frontier outward.
questions.hint: Resources, technology, and human capital drive growth.
